scope: Twenty individually checked existing AS school-mock short flashcards: 10 AQA Physics measurement/free-fall/Young modulus practical recall and 10 AQA Chemistry calorimetry/enthalpy practical recall.
purpose: Make real flashcard markers accept valid concise science answers while rejecting key measurement and calorimetry misconceptions; support the user's currently unverified full-practical reasoning skills without pretending that recall alone certifies a practical exam.
preservation: Original question/model answer/saved IDs and bank indices unchanged. v354 extra bank and all prior supplement banks remain loaded.
limitations: These are 20 reviewed existing cards, not completion of AQA's full mock specification.
Full uncertainty calculations, practical evaluation, drawing graphs and drawn experimental diagrams still need separate written-exam practice/manual assessment.
Passing known examples does not guarantee every unseen paraphrase will be accepted.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is resolution?
rows.originalBack: The smallest change an instrument can distinguish.
accept: Resolution is the minimum change that a measuring device can detect.
The smallest discernible difference in the measured quantity.
reject: Resolution is how close a measurement is to its true value.
Resolution means the spread between repeated measurements.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is repeatability?
rows.originalBack: Same result using the same method, equipment and operator.
accept: Repeatability means consistent readings with the same person, method and apparatus.
Measurements agree when repeated by the same operator with unchanged equipment and method.
reject: Repeatability means measurements agree between different laboratories using different apparatus.
Repeatability is the difference between an observed measurement and the true value.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is reproducibility?
rows.originalBack: Consistent results when the method is repeated under changed conditions.
accept: Reproducibility means results agree when the measurement is repeated under changed conditions, such as a different operator.
Similar results with different people or equipment show reproducibility.
reject: Reproducibility requires the exact same observer and apparatus every time.
It means a single measurement is exactly equal to the true value.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is precision in measurements?
rows.originalBack: How close repeated readings are to one another.
accept: Precise repeated measurements cluster closely together.
Precision describes the small spread of readings taken repeatedly.
reject: Precision means closeness to the accepted true value, regardless of spread.
Precision is simply the smallest scale division of an instrument.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is accuracy in measurements?
rows.originalBack: How close a measured value is to the true value.
accept: Accuracy is closeness of the measured value to the accepted true value.
A measurement is accurate if it is close to the actual value.
reject: Accuracy means repeated readings are close to one another, even far from the true value.
Accuracy is simply the number of decimal places shown.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For quantities added, how do absolute uncertainties combine?
rows.originalBack: Add their absolute uncertainties.
accept: Add the individual absolute uncertainties when adding two measured quantities.
For a sum, combined absolute uncertainty equals the sum of the absolute uncertainties.
reject: Multiply all absolute uncertainties together for quantities added.
Subtract the smaller absolute uncertainty from the larger one.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For a measured quantity squared, what happens to its percentage uncertainty?
rows.originalBack: Double it.
accept: The squared quantity has twice the percentage uncertainty.
Multiplying a measured quantity by itself doubles its fractional or percentage uncertainty.
reject: Square the percentage uncertainty to get the percentage uncertainty of the squared quantity.
The percentage uncertainty is halved when a quantity is squared.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does the gradient of distance against time squared represent for free fall from rest?
accept: The slope of distance against time squared equals half the acceleration due to gravity.
For s plotted against t² from rest, gradient = ½g.
reject: The gradient is 2g for distance against time squared.
The slope is g rather than g/2.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Which graph gives Young modulus as its gradient?
rows.originalBack: Tensile stress against tensile strain.
accept: The gradient of a stress-versus-strain graph in its elastic linear region is Young modulus.
Plot tensile stress on the vertical axis against tensile strain horizontally; its initial linear gradient gives E.
reject: The slope of force against extension alone directly equals Young modulus without length or area corrections.
The gradient of a displacement-time graph equals Young modulus.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why measure a wire's diameter at several positions?
rows.originalBack: To reduce random error and check for variation.
accept: Measure the diameter several times along the wire to average random variation and identify uneven thickness.
Multiple position measurements reveal variations in diameter and reduce uncertainty in the mean.
reject: To increase the wire diameter by measuring it repeatedly.
It is unnecessary to check variations because every point on a real wire has precisely the same diameter.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What equation relates heat, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature rise?
rows.originalBack: q=mcΔT with q in J, m in g, c in J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
accept: q = m c ΔT, heat energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change.
Use q=mcΔT, with mass in g and c in J per g per kelvin to give q in joules.
reject: q = mc/ΔT.
q = mΔT/c.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How is ΔT calculated from initial and final temperatures?
rows.originalBack: ΔT=T_final−T_initial; changes in °C and K are numerically equal.
accept: Temperature change equals final temperature minus initial temperature, and a degree Celsius rise equals a kelvin rise.
ΔT=Tfinal−Tinitial; a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.
reject: ΔT is always initial minus final temperature.
A temperature increase of 1 °C is equal to 274 K of temperature change.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: When liquid density is 1 g cm⁻³, how does mass relate to volume?
rows.originalBack: Solution mass in grams approximately equals its volume in cm³.
accept: At density 1 g/cm³, a volume of V cm³ has approximately V g mass.
Mass in grams equals volume in cm³ when density is 1 g per cubic centimetre.
reject: Mass in g is one thousand times the volume in cm³ at density 1 g/cm³.
Mass in grams is the volume in cm³ divided by 1000 at this density.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: In a solution calorimeter, what mass usually goes in q=mcΔT?
rows.originalBack: Mass of the solution that changes temperature, not only the solute.
accept: Use the mass of the whole solution that undergoes the temperature change, rather than the dissolved solute alone.
The total heated or cooled solution mass goes into q=mcΔT.
reject: Use only the mass of the solute, not the solution.
Ignore the solution mass entirely and use the mass of the dry container.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is ΔH negative if the solution warms?
rows.originalBack: The solution gains heat, so the reaction has released it.
accept: The solution gains energy from an exothermic reaction, so the reaction enthalpy change is negative.
Because the solution warms, heat has been released by the reaction and ΔH is below zero.
reject: If a solution gets warmer the chemical reaction must absorb heat and have positive ΔH.
The reaction enthalpy is positive because its solution gains heat.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is ΔH positive if the solution cools?
rows.originalBack: The solution loses heat; the reaction absorbs heat from surroundings.
accept: A cooling solution supplies heat to an endothermic reaction, so reaction ΔH is positive.
The reaction absorbs energy from the surroundings, the solution temperature falls, and ΔH is above zero.
reject: A cooling solution means the reaction released energy with negative ΔH.
The reaction is exothermic because the solution temperature fell.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the purpose of a calorimeter's insulation?
rows.originalBack: To reduce heat transfer between system and external surroundings.
accept: Insulation limits heat loss to or heat gain from the external surroundings.
It minimises unwanted heat transfer between the calorimeter system and its environment.
reject: Insulation is used to increase heat exchange with the surroundings.
Its purpose is to stop any temperature change occurring in the solution.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What happens when an endothermic experiment gains external heat?
rows.originalBack: Temperature fall is too small; measured ΔH is underestimated in magnitude.
accept: Heat entering from outside reduces the observed cooling and underestimates the magnitude of endothermic ΔH.
An external heat gain makes ΔT less negative and the calculated endothermic enthalpy smaller.
reject: External heat makes the solution cool more and overestimates the endothermic enthalpy magnitude.
Heat gained from outside cannot affect the measured temperature fall.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does extrapolating a temperature–time graph estimate?
rows.originalBack: Corrected temperature at the mixing/reaction time, reducing heat-exchange error.
accept: Extrapolate the temperature trend back to the instant of mixing to estimate a heat-loss-corrected temperature.
The extrapolated graph gives the estimated temperature at reaction or mixing time without later heat exchange.
reject: Extrapolate to the temperature after the mixture has completely cooled to room temperature.
Extrapolation changes how many moles of reactant reacted rather than the temperature estimate.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does n mean in ΔH = −q/n?
rows.originalBack: Moles of the reaction as written, or of the species named in the definition.
accept: n is the reaction amount in moles as written, or the number of moles of the species used to define ΔH.
Use moles of reaction with balanced coefficients or moles of the substance named by the enthalpy definition.
reject: n must always be the mass of the reactant in grams.
n is always the number of moles of water, regardless of which enthalpy change is defined.
